questions.question: What is a statement with a truth value?
questions.explanation: Propositions can be true or false.

questions.question: What are the two truth values?
questions.explanation: Logic uses True and False values.

questions.question: What connects propositions with AND?
questions.explanation: Conjunction joins statements with AND.

questions.question: What symbol represents negation?
questions.explanation: ¬ inverts the truth value.

questions.question: What connects propositions with OR?
questions.explanation: Disjunction joins statements with OR.

questions.question: What is a compound proposition?
questions.explanation: Compound propositions combine simpler ones.

questions.question: What is always true?
questions.explanation: Tautologies are always true.

questions.question: What is always false?
questions.explanation: Contradictions are always false.

questions.question: What symbol represents conjunction?
questions.explanation: ∧ represents logical AND.

questions.question: What symbol represents disjunction?
questions.explanation: ∨ represents logical OR.

questions.question: Which of the following is a proposition?
options: The Earth revolves around the Sun.
questions.explanation: Only declarative sentences with a definite truth value are propositions; commands, questions, and exclamations are not.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a proposition?
options: Paris is the capital of France.
questions.explanation: x + 3 = 10 is an open sentence; its truth value depends on the value assigned to x.

questions.question: The statement 'If it rains, then the ground gets wet' is what kind of proposition?
questions.explanation: It combines two atomic propositions using the implication connective.

questions.question: What is the truth value of p→q when p is false and q is false?
questions.explanation: An implication with a false antecedent is vacuously true, regardless of the consequent.

questions.question: What is the truth value of p→q when p is true and q is false?
questions.explanation: A true antecedent with a false consequent is the only case where an implication is false.

questions.question: A proposition that is true in some rows and false in others of its truth table is called what?
questions.explanation: A contingency is neither always true nor always false.

questions.question: What is the converse of p→q?
questions.explanation: The converse swaps the hypothesis and conclusion without negating.

questions.question: What is the inverse of p→q?
questions.explanation: The inverse negates both the hypothesis and the conclusion.

questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to p→q?
questions.explanation: An implication is equivalent only to its contrapositive ¬q→¬p.

questions.question: When is the biconditional p↔q true?
options: When p and q have different truth values
When p and q have the same truth value
Only when both p and q are true
Only when both p and q are false
questions.explanation: The biconditional is true whenever both operands match, including the false-false case.

questions.question: When is p⊕q (exclusive OR) true?
options: When both p and q are true
When p and q have different truth values
When both p and q are false
questions.explanation: XOR is true exactly when one operand is true and the other is false.

questions.question: Given p=True, q=False, r=True, what is the value of (p∨q)∧r?
questions.explanation: p∨q = T∨F = T, then T∧T = T.

questions.question: Given p=True, q=True, r=False, what is the value of p→(q∧r)?
questions.explanation: q∧r = T∧F = F, so p→F with p true evaluates to False.

questions.question: In English, 'p if q' translates to which implication?
questions.explanation: 'p if q' means q is a sufficient condition for p, i.e. q→p.

questions.question: In English, 'p only if q' translates to which implication?
questions.explanation: 'p only if q' means q is a necessary condition for p, i.e. p→q.

questions.question: What does the symbol ⊥ (bottom, falsum) denote?
questions.explanation: ⊥ is the logical constant that is false under every interpretation.

questions.question: A DPLL solver holds clauses (p∨q), (¬p∨r), (¬q∨¬r) and assigns p=False. What does unit propagation force next?
questions.explanation: p=F makes (p∨q) unit, forcing q=T; then (¬q∨¬r) becomes unit, forcing r=F — and (¬p∨r) stays satisfied.

questions.question: Resolving the clauses (¬p∨q) and (p∨r) on the variable p produces which clause?
questions.explanation: Resolution drops the complementary literals p and ¬p and merges the rest: q∨r.

questions.question: Under p=True, q=False, r=True, what is the value of (p↔q)→(r⊕¬q)?
questions.explanation: p↔q = T↔F = F; r⊕¬q = T⊕T = F; F→F = T.

questions.question: Which is the correct CNF of p↔q?
questions.explanation: p↔q = (p→q)∧(q→p) = (¬p∨q)∧(¬q∨p) — two clauses, each a disjunction.

questions.question: Classify the formula (p→q)↔(¬q→¬p).
options: Tautology — contraposition holds in all 4 rows
questions.explanation: An implication always equals its contrapositive, so the biconditional is true in every row.
